extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate counsel, patent prosecutors, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and tests applied by the Federal Circuit on appeal in patent litigation — covering claim construction, infringement fact review, obviousness/anticipation, indefiniteness, evidentiary credibility, and related procedural rules (statute of limitations, jury demand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for factual findings (clear error)
rubrics_metrics.description: We review that finding of fact for clear error, and we reverse only if “on the entire evidence [we are] left with the definite and firm conviction that a mistake has been committed.” Biovail Corp. Int'l v. Andrx Pharms., Inc., 239 F.3d 1297, 1300 (Fed. Cir. 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual determinations (e.g., whether disputed strings are anchored in the 'corner' vs 'side') are reviewed deferentially; appellants must show a definite and firm conviction of error to reverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim indefiniteness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid invalidity for indefiniteness, a claim, read in light of the specification, must “reasonably apprise those skilled in the art both of the utilization and scope of the invention.” Shatterproof Glass Corp. v. Libbey-Owens-Ford Co., 758 F.2d 613, 624 (Fed. Cir. 1985).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim 'is subject to construction, i.e., it is not insolubly ambiguous, it is not invalid for indefiniteness.' Bancorp Servs., L.L.C. v. Hartford Life Ins. Co., 359 F.3d 1367, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2004). A claim will not be held invalid if its meaning is discernible even though reasonable persons may disagree; courts look to specification and figures to supply sufficient basis for construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using specification and figures in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and the figures provide a sufficient basis for differentiating 'sides' from 'corners' (e.g., 'sides' contain only lateral string ends; 'corners' contain both lateral and longitudinal string ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may construe terms by reference to the written description and figures when they instruct how to differentiate portions of the claimed device; ordinary-language terms that are not used in a specialized sense ('region') may be interpreted by their plain meaning as used in the spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation and inherency (what prior art must disclose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference that is silent about a limitation (e.g., direction in which opposite ends of a string are splayed) does not necessarily anticipate; inherency requires that the asserted limitation be necessarily present in the prior art disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art does not inherently disclose every limitation (e.g., does not disclose whether splay is in opposite directions or number of main strings), it may not anticipate the claim; board/examiner analysis on anticipation focuses on presence or absence of explicit or necessarily present disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis and combining prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court concluded that using an even number of strings would have been an obvious way of implementing Martel, given that all commercial tennis racquets on the market contained an even number of strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may rely on what would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art, including market practice; obviousness can be found by combining the disclosure of a reference with common design choices unless a reference explicitly suggests otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away concept in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: AAI argued Martel teaches away from the claimed invention because it calls for a racquet design that limits twisting, which AAI says an even number of strings would cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teaching-away argument can defeat an obviousness combination, but the party asserting teaching away must explain why the prior art discourages the claimed modification; unsupported assertions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of PTO reexamination/Board findings on court validity analysis (Portola distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portola Packaging holds that in reexamination the PTO should not reevaluate prior art considered in original examination, but Portola does not limit a court’s authority to consider prior art that was before the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Board decision reversing an examiner on anticipation does not preclude a court from addressing obviousness; reexamination procedural limits on the PTO are distinct from a court's authority to adjudicate validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of claim language when term is not specialized ('region')
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification makes clear that the term 'region' is not used in a specialized sense, but merely refers to a portion of the edge of the racquet, so the claim language 'in the regions where the length of said ends is greater' equates to 'where the length of said ends is greater.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary words used in their plain sense in the specification do not introduce fatal ambiguity; courts may simplify or equate such language to its plain counterpart for construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing-breach doctrine and trade-secret-related contract claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuing-breach theory does not apply to breach of a contract covering trade secrets; where contract claims 'consist entirely of the same acts of misappropriation . . . that would be barred by the statute of limitations applicable to trade secret claims,' they cannot be revived by treating each act as a continuing breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Arizona law (as applied here), misappropriation of trade secrets has a 3-year statute of limitations and 'a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim'; plaintiffs cannot extend contract claims beyond the statutory period by recasting them as continuing breaches when they are essentially trade-secret misappropriation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations tolling during related litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: AAI argued the statute should be tolled during the pendency of an earlier lawsuit because the action involving the ’731 patent was stayed; the court rejected this because AAI's trade secret claim had been voluntarily dismissed earlier and AAI pointed to no authority for tolling under these facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolling during earlier litigation is not automatic; a party must identify legal authority supporting tolling and the factual predicate (e.g., an actual stayed claim) to justify tolling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility determinations for expert witnesses (deferential review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the district court acknowledged the expert’s credibility was 'significantly clouded' by counsel’s 'extensive involvement' in preparing the report, it nonetheless credited the expert’s testimony due to his expertise and qualifications. Appellate review of such credibility determinations is highly deferential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial-court credibility assessments are given substantial deference on appeal; even significant clouding may not compel reversal if the court found the expert otherwise credible and qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of jury demand (FRCP 38(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court ruled that AAI forfeited its right to a jury trial when it failed to serve its jury demand on Prince in a timely manner, as required by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to serve a timely jury demand results in forfeiture; courts generally will not excuse failures that result from mere oversight or inadvertence unless the party shows some reason beyond oversight (citing Ninth Circuit authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a claim 'is subject to construction' it is not fatally indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim 'is subject to construction, i.e., it is not insolubly ambiguous, it is not invalid for indefiniteness.' Bancorp Servs., L.L.C. v. Hartford Life Ins. Co., 359 F.3d 1367, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2004).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even difficult claim-construction tasks do not equate to indefiniteness; discernible meaning suffices—courts must attempt construction before finding invalidity for indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of industry practice and common commercial design in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court observed that all commercial tennis racquets on the market contained an even number of strings and therefore concluded that using an even number would have been an obvious implementation of Martel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established industry practice and the prevalence of certain design choices can be relevant to what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.
